Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test `testRevert()` creates a Line instance from two points, then expects the direction of the reverted line to be the negation of the original line's direction using Vector3D.negate(). The bug report states that the method currently used, Line.revert(), is imprecise because it only maintains ~10 digits for the direction vector, which causes precision problems for lines far from the origin.

Inspecting the Line.revert() method shows this imprecision: the method creates a new line using a zero vector (field zero) and a direction vector computed by subtracting from zero. This "zero.subtract(direction)" approach loses precision. The zero field in Line is a Vector3D that is an origin point for the line's representation.

The constructor Line(Vector3D, Vector3D) calls reset(), which normalizes the direction vector and calculates another reference vector zero. Thus, constructing the line with zero.subtract(direction) will cause repeated rounding errors in reset() due to large magnitude components and normalization.

In contrast, Vector3D.negate() returns an exact negation of each coordinate of the direction vector, preserving precision.

Hence, the root cause is that Line.revert() constructs a new Line with zero and zero.subtract(direction) rather than reusing negate() on the direction vector directly. This leads to precision loss in the test, which expects an accurate negation of the direction vector.

Additionally, the bug report questions why Line is mutable when it only consists of two vectors, potentially allowing for immutable design and preventing such errors by design.

Therefore, the bug in the revert() method implementation matching the symptoms in the test is confirmed.

Next, I will suggest which methods should be the best locations to be fixed.
